title: Two Loners Among Pairs
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Exactly two values appear once; every other value appears exactly twice. Return the two values that appear once, in any order.

Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space, so no hash map.

examples.why: 4 and 1 each appear twice. [6, 9] is also accepted.
Nothing is paired; both values are loners. Negative numbers are allowed.
XOR of everything gives 3 ^ 7 = 4, so bit 2 splits them: 7 has it, 3 does not.

constraints: Exactly two values appear once; all others appear exactly twice
hints: XOR of a value with itself is 0. What does XOR of the whole array leave behind?
You get a ^ b. Since a ≠ b, at least one bit is set in it. What does that bit tell you about a and b?
Pick one set bit of a ^ b, for example the lowest one. Split the array by that bit and XOR each group separately: pairs still cancel, and a and b land in different groups.

explain.intuition:
XOR-ing every number cancels the pairs and leaves x = a ^ b. That is not yet the answer, but it is a clue: a bit that is 1 in x is a bit where a and b differ.

Take one such bit, say the lowest set bit x & -x. Every number either has that bit or not. Both copies of a paired value go to the same side, so they still cancel inside their group. a and b go to different sides. XOR-ing each group now leaves exactly one loner per group.
steps: XOR all numbers into x; this equals a ^ b.
Take bit = x & -x, the lowest bit where a and b differ.
XOR together all numbers that have bit set; the result is one loner.
pitfalls: Overflow when computing x & -x in a language with fixed-width ints and x = INT_MIN. In JavaScript the bit operators work on 32-bit ints, so it is safe; in Python mask to 32 bits or use the unbounded int directly.
Splitting by the highest bit of x with Math.log2: negative numbers make that wrong. Lowest set bit is simpler.
Forgetting that 0 can be one of the loners. The XOR trick handles it; a check like if (first) does not.

solutions.title: Count with a hash map
solutions.idea: Count every value, return those with count 1. Easy, but uses O(n) space.

solutions.title: XOR and split by a differing bit
solutions.idea: XOR of all gives a ^ b. Any set bit of it separates a from b, so XOR each side separately.

followups: Every value appears three times except one. How do you find it with bit counting?
What if three values appear once and the rest twice? Does one split still suffice?
